newsitem.title: GERMANY: German speaker says rivals using smear tactics.
newsitem.headline: German speaker says rivals using smear tactics.

text.p: Germany's beleaguered parliamentary speaker Rita Suessmuth, under fire over allegations she misused official aircraft, said on Sunday political rivals were responsible for a smear campaign against her.
Suessmuth, Germany's top woman politician, told the newspaper Welt am Sonntag she had paid for private visits to Zurich out of her own pocket and used military transport planes only for business.

Suessmuth's daughter lives in Zurich and a German taxpayers' association has demanded a full accounting of 31 flights -- mostly at weekends -- that Suessmuth took to or from Switzerland since January 1993.

The newspaper reported that Suessmuth had taken 14 additional military flights costing more than 100,000 marks ($64,220) in the last three years to an airport in the Netherlands not far from where she owns a vacation house.
Suessmuth denied the new allegation in a statement released in Bonn on Sunday by the parliamentary press office. She said she had never taken a military transport ride for a private holiday.

"I paid for my private trips on Lufthansa and Swissair just like any other private citizen," Suessmuth said. "These checks are necessary. But campaigns like this are aimed at causing permanent damage."
In another interview with Deutsche Welle television, Suessmuth said: "I am angry and enraged because they can really destroy people with campaigns like this."

It was the first time Suessmuth, known as the "Mrs Clean" of German politics for her preaching style, had openly suggested what many in Bonn suspected -- that enemies from within her own Christian Democratic (CDU) party and its Bavarian sister CSU party were responsible for leaking the embarrassing details to the media.
Suessmuth, 59, is a former university professor from the liberal wing of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's CDU and has many foes, especially among more conservative elements of the party.
Kohl denied on Thursday that he or other party leaders wanted to discredit her.
Suessmuth is disliked by some politicians because of her advocacy of women's issues and what many conservatives see as her moralising stand on social questions.

Markus Soeder, head of the conservative Christian Social Union (CSU) youth wing in Bavaria, told the newspaper Bild am Sonntag that Suessmuth should resign if it turned out that she had used even one official flight for private business.
"Rita Suessmuth should accept the consequences and resign if even one trip with military aircraft was for private affairs," Soeder said.

Bild, which has published new allegations against Suessmuth all week, said on Sunday it had found evidence that she took a military plane at a cost of more than 16,000 marks to Zurich on October 23 to attend her daughter's graduation ceremony.

"This is a clear violation of the guidelines," said Dieter Lau, vice president of the taxpayer association. "The military flights can only be used for official business. And that certainly does not include private graduation parties."
Suessmuth also took many military flights between Zurich and Bonn even though there were seats available on scheduled commercial flights between the two cities, Bild said.

The weekly news magazine Der Spiegel reported in its latest edition that Suessmuth defended one military flight from Tuebingen in southern Germany to Zurich by saying it would have cost more if she had travelled to her home near the northern city of Hanover.
"So what can you say against that?" she asked.

Welt am Sonntag found that Suessmuth had made 90 short- and middle-distance flights between 1993 and 1996 using military aircraft. It said she had made more such flights than Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel.
